cards.name: trigger_recency
cards.mechanism: Intent decays in real time, not in list positions. For each of u's last 15 items of the last 90 steps, take up to 20 of that item's most recent other adopters and see whether they took candidate j. This yields three signals: the age in steps of u's most recent item that leads to j (is the related interest still live?), a co-adoption share decayed by exp(-age/7) in actual steps, and the number of distinct visits (active steps) of u that contain a trigger of j. The last one marks an interest u keeps returning to. Existing cooc_last5 and cooc_wsum weight by position, so they treat a 20-item haul from yesterday the same as 20 single visits spread over months.
cards.stratum: users whose history mixes recent and older visits, so trigger ages differ: u has at least 2 distinct active steps in [A-90, A) and an event in the last 14 steps. cards.name: visit_day_context
cards.mechanism: What was being bought on the exact steps when u last shopped (u's last 3 active steps) captures the context of u's current intent: promotions, drops and campaigns that u was exposed to. The share of that day's active users who took j, and its lift over j's current 30-step share, separate items that were hot at u's moment from items that are hot in general.
cards.stratum: users who shopped recently, so their visit-day context is still current: last event within 14 steps. SQL: (SELECT max(e.t) FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = cand.user_id) >= {A} - 14
cards.null_stratum: dormant users whose last visit was long ago; that context is stale. SQL: (SELECT max(e.t) FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = cand.user_id) < {A} - 90

cards.name: exposure_since_launch
cards.mechanism: Skipped exposure versus unseen novelty. The first column counts how many of u's visits in the last 180 steps happened after j's first event, i.e. visits where u could have taken j and did not. The second gives the share of those visits on which j was actually being bought by others that same step. A low count marks a new arrival that u has not had a chance to see, and such items should rank high. Many co-present visits without adoption mark an item u keeps passing by.
cards.stratum: frequent visitors, for whom exposure counts vary across candidates: at least 4 distinct active steps in [A-180, A). SQL: (SELECT count(DISTINCT e.t) FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = cand.user_id AND e.t >= {A} - 180) >= 4
cards.null_stratum: users with no visit in the last 180 steps; both columns are 0 for every candidate. SQL: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = cand.user_id AND e.t >= {A} - 180)

cards.name: recency_state_pop
cards.mechanism: Users who come back after a pause of a given length buy different things than users in a streak. Returners after a long gap take new-season basics and bestsellers, while users in a burst take complements. Every session in the last 60 steps is bucketed by its gap since the previous active step (log2 buckets, plus a bucket for no visit in the prior year). The family measures j's share among sessions in the bucket matching u's current elapsed pause, and j's lift in that bucket over all sessions.
cards.stratum: users in a non-typical state, either dormant or in a streak: user_recency >= 32 or <= 1. SQL: {A} - (SELECT max(e.t) FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = cand.user_id) >= 32 OR {A} - (SELECT max(e.t) FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = cand.user_id) <= 1
cards.null_stratum: users with a moderate pause of 4 to 16 steps, whose bucket resembles the overall session mix so the lift is about 0. SQL: {A} - (SELECT max(e.t) FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = cand.user_id) BETWEEN 4 AND 16

cards.name: session_state
cards.mechanism: The shape of the user's latest visit: the number of distinct items taken at the last active step (a haul versus a single targeted pick) and the gap before that visit (a streak versus a return after a pause). Haul shoppers and returners spread over popular, broad items, while targeted shoppers in a streak follow co-occurrence. The trees can use this state to switch between the popularity and similarity features.
cards.stratum: users whose last visit was a haul or followed a long pause: last-step item count >= 4 or previous gap >= 60. SQL: (SELECT count(*) FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = users.user_id AND e.t = (SELECT max(e2.t) FROM ev e2 WHERE e2.user_id = users.user_id)) >= 4
cards.null_stratum: users with a single active step in total, for whom prev_gap is the default and the haul size equals n_items_all. SQL: (SELECT count(DISTINCT e.t) FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = users.user_id) = 1

cards.name: pace_aligned_momentum
cards.mechanism: Each user's relevant trend horizon is their own rhythm. A user who visits every 2 steps reacts to what surged in the last 2 steps, and a monthly user to the last month. The horizon h is the power of 2 (1 to 32) closest above u's median gap between distinct active steps in the last 365 steps. The family measures j's per-step demand in [A-h, A) relative to its 60-step per-step demand, a momentum at the user's own timescale that fixed windows like users_7/users_30 cannot express.
cards.stratum: users with a very short or very long rhythm (median gap <= 2 or >= 16), where h differs most from the fixed 7- and 30-step windows. SQL: users whose median gap between distinct active steps in the last 365 steps is <= 2 or >= 16
cards.null_stratum: users with a median gap of about 5 to 8 steps, where h = 8 makes the column nearly a rescaled trend. SQL: users whose median gap between distinct active steps in [A-365, A) is between 5 and 8

cards.name: missed_since_visit
cards.mechanism: What happened to j while u was away: the adopters of j strictly after u's last active step (log count), and their share of j's lifetime adopters. A share of 1 means j launched after u's last visit, so it is a novelty u has never seen. A high count since the visit means demand u missed and will meet on return. This is a per-user window ending at u's own last visit, which none of the fixed-anchor windows capture.

cards.name: cohort_expected_growth
cards.mechanism: Items follow a typical life-cycle curve: launch ramp, plateau, decay. The family learns that curve empirically from the previous horizon. For every item at A-30 it takes the age bucket (log2 age), audience bucket (log2 users in [A-60,A-30)) and direction (sign of the change versus [A-90,A-60)), and the realised log growth into [A-30,A). The result is a forward estimate of the item's growth into the next 30 steps, conditioned jointly on life stage and level. Single-item ratios like trend or momentum only extrapolate an item's own past and miss the typical turn of the curve.

cards.null_stratum: Old items, more than 365 steps since launch, on a flat part of the curve: item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM ev GROUP BY item_id HAVING min(t) < {A} - 365)

cards.mechanism: Item silence means different things depending on the item's own rhythm. cards.null_stratum: Items with events in the last 2 steps, whose ratio is near-constant: item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM ev WHERE t >= {A} - 2 GROUP BY item_id)

cards.name: lastyear_phase_transition
cards.mechanism: Seasonal demand is sequential, not just a level effect: what people buy after item i in spring differs from what they buy after it in autumn. For each of u's last 10 items i, the family takes the users who took i in [A-395, A-365), one cycle before the current phase. cards.name: pair_order_profile
cards.mechanism: Direction and simultaneity of the edge i-j among co-users in the last 120 steps, pooled over u's last 10 items i. after_share is the smoothed share of the ordered co-user pairs in which j came strictly after i. same_step_share is the share of co-users who took i and j in the same step. This is graph smoothing of trend: it gives a trend estimate to items whose own counts are too small to be stable. The id-adjacency trend already in the model uses catalog order, not the behavioural graph.

cards.mechanism: How tightly u's last 10 items cluster in the 180-step co-occurrence graph. hist_cohesion is the mean pairwise cosine over all pairs. chain_support is the share of consecutive items (by recency) linked by an edge with sim > 0. Cohesive, chain-like users move along graph edges, so their next items are well predicted by the cooc features. Scattered users jump across the graph and are better served by popularity. As a user-level gate, the family lets the trees decide per user how much weight the many pair-level graph scores deserve.

cards.null_stratum: Users with exactly 1 item, which has no pairs (NaN): (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id) = 1

cards.name: neighbours_since_last_visit
cards.mechanism: A user-user neighbourhood anchored to the user's own clock. The neighbours of u are the top 30 users by cosine overlap with u's last 20 items in the last 90 steps. The value is the sim-weighted share of these neighbours who took j strictly after u's last interaction. A returning user tends to catch up on what their taste community adopted while they were away. A fixed 30-step window, as in ag_ucf30, mixes items that u has already passed over (adopted by neighbours while u was active and ignored) with items that are new to u. Cutting at u's last step separates the two.

cards.null_stratum: Users active in the last step, for whom nothing can happen after their last step and the value is 0: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id AND t >= {A} - 1)

cards.name: item_successor_role
cards.mechanism: The position of an item in the transition graph. followup_share is the smoothed share of j's adoptions in the last 120 steps that came within 30 steps after the adopter's previous active step, so j has strong in-edges from other purchases. entry_share is the share of adoptions made in the adopter's very first step, an entry or source node. Every ranked user already has history, so the next item is by construction a transition from an earlier one. Items that are typically reached as follow-ups should rank higher than acquisition and entry items, which mostly attract new users and are counted by popularity anyway.
cards.stratum: Users in follow-up mode, active within the last 30 steps: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id AND t >= {A} - 30)
cards.null_stratum: Long-lapsed users who behave close to new entrants: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id AND t >= {A} - 90)

cards.name: heat_conduction_niche
cards.mechanism: Heat-conduction (HeatS) diffusion on the 90-step user-item bipartite graph. Resource flows from u's last 20 items to their co-users v with weight 1/k_v, then to j, and is averaged over j's degree: score = sum_i sum_{v has i and j} (1/k_v) / n(j). This is the share of j's audience that consists of light co-users of the user's items, roughly P(i|j). Cosine and P(j|i) reward items that the user's region often reaches. HeatS rewards niche items whose whole audience lies inside the user's region. Such long-tail candidates are the ones popularity features push down.

cards.mechanism: Each user's relevant trend horizon is their own rhythm. A user who visits every 2 steps reacts to what surged in the last 2 steps, and a monthly user to the last month. cards.mechanism: Items follow a typical life-cycle curve: launch ramp, plateau, decay. The family learns that curve empirically from the previous horizon. The result is a forward estimate of the item's growth into the next 30 steps, conditioned jointly on life stage and level. Single-item ratios like trend or momentum only extrapolate an item's own past and miss the typical turn of the curve.

cards.mechanism: Item silence means different things depending on the item's own rhythm. The dormancy ratio relates the steps since j's last event to j's mean gap between active steps over its lifetime. The longest historical gap between active steps marks items that have gone dark and come back before (restocks, recurring drops). Such items can revive in the next 30 steps even when currently silent. item_last alone cannot separate these cases.

cards.name: pair_order_profile
cards.mechanism: Direction and simultaneity of the edge i-j among co-users in the last 120 steps, pooled over u's last 10 items i. after_share is the smoothed share of the ordered co-user pairs in which j came strictly after i. same_step_share is the share of co-users who took i and j in the same step. rival.explanation: after_share is high whenever j was released after i, because no co-user can take j before it exists. The column may therefore only encode the item-age difference, a freshness preference, and not any behavioural order.
rival.stratum: Young candidates: (SELECT {A} - MIN(t) FROM ev WHERE ev.item_id = j.item_id) <= 30

cards.name: basket_markov_2step
cards.mechanism: A first-order Markov chain over consecutive active steps (baskets) of every user in the last 180 steps: P(j|i) = transitions from i in basket s to j in the user's next basket, divided by all transitions out of i. The card runs a two-step walk from u's last basket, using each seed's top-20 successors as intermediate states: score = sum over seeds and k of ws * P(k|seed) * P(j|k). Step units are unknown and visits are irregular, so 'two purchases from now' is counted in baskets, not in steps. The label window of 30 steps usually spans more than one future basket. The existing transitions are one-hop and time-windowed. This column scores what tends to come in the basket after next.
cards.stratum: Users active within the last 30 steps, whose next baskets are likely to fall inside the window: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id AND t >= {A} - 30)
cards.null_stratum: Users whose last basket is older than 180 steps, where the chain has no transitions from the seeds: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id AND t >= {A} - 180)

rival.explanation: Two-step mass collects on items with a large in-degree in the transition graph, which are popular follow-up items. The gain could therefore come from popularity among active repeat buyers, not from the chain's personal path.
rival.stratum: Candidates with at least 20 distinct users in the last 30 steps: (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev WHERE ev.item_id = j.item_id AND t >= {A} - 30) >= 20

cards.name: graph_neighbourhood_momentum
cards.mechanism: Demand travels along the co-adoption graph: when the complements and close substitutes of an item heat up, the item follows. For item j, take its top-20 cosine neighbours on the 60-step graph, built from users with at most 100 items in that window so that heavy users do not dominate. Two columns follow. One is the sim-weighted 7-to-30 ratio of the neighbours' audience. The other is the log ratio of the neighbours' 30-step audience to their audience in [A-60, A-30). This is graph smoothing of trend: it gives a trend estimate to items whose own counts are too small to be stable. The id-adjacency trend already in the model uses catalog order, not the behavioural graph.
cards.stratum: Candidates with a small own recent audience, where their own users_7/users_30 ratio is noise: (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev WHERE ev.item_id = j.item_id AND t >= {A} - 30) BETWEEN 1 AND 5
cards.null_stratum: Candidates without events in the last 60 steps, which have no graph neighbours and get NaN: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.item_id = j.item_id AND t >= {A} - 60)
cards.sql: WITH e AS (SELECT user_id, item_id, t FROM ev WHERE t >= {A} - 60), e2 AS (SELECT user_id, item_id FROM e QUALIFY COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) <= 100), n AS (SELECT item_id, COUNT(*) AS c FROM e2 GROUP BY item_id), co AS (SELECT a.item_id AS j, b.item_id AS k, COUNT(*) AS c FROM e2 a JOIN e2 b ON b.user_id = a.user_id AND b.item_id <> a.item_id GROUP BY a.item_id, b.item_id), nb AS (SELECT co.j, co.k, co.c / SQRT(nj.c * nk.c) AS w FROM co JOIN n nj ON nj.item_id = co.j JOIN n nk ON nk.item_id = co.k QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY co.j ORDER BY co.c / SQRT(nj.c * nk.c) DESC, co.k) <= 20), pop AS (SELECT item_id, SUM(CASE WHEN t >= {A} - 7 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS u7, SUM(CASE WHEN t >= {A} - 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS u30, SUM(CASE WHEN t < {A} - 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS u60 FROM e GROUP BY item_id) SELECT nb.j AS item_id, SUM(nb.w * pop.u7) / NULLIF(SUM(nb.w * pop.u30), 0) AS f_x_c3_nbr_trend7, LN((1 + SUM(nb.w * pop.u30)) / (1 + SUM(nb.w * pop.u60))) AS f_x_c3_nbr_mom30 FROM nb JOIN pop ON pop.item_id = nb.k GROUP BY nb.j;

rival.explanation: Graph neighbours share most of their audience with j, so their trend may only repeat j's own trend with less noise. That would make the family a denoised copy of trend and ag_mom_30_60 and not a carrier of new information.
rival.stratum: Candidates with a large own audience, where their own trend is already precise: (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev WHERE ev.item_id = j.item_id AND t >= {A} - 30) >= 50

cards.name: history_cohesion
cards.mechanism: How tightly u's last 10 items cluster in the 180-step co-occurrence graph. hist_cohesion is the mean pairwise cosine over all pairs. chain_support is the share of consecutive items (by recency) linked by an edge with sim > 0. Cohesive, chain-like users move along graph edges, so their next items are well predicted by the cooc features. Scattered users jump across the graph and are better served by popularity. As a user-level gate, the family lets the trees decide per user how much weight the many pair-level graph scores deserve.
cards.stratum: Users with at least 5 items, for whom cohesion is well defined and varies: (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id) >= 5
cards.null_stratum: Users with exactly 1 item, which has no pairs (NaN): (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id) = 1
cards.sql: WITH e AS (SELECT user_id, item_id FROM ev WHERE t >= {A} - 180), n AS (SELECT item_id, COUNT(*) AS c FROM e GROUP BY item_id), s AS (SELECT user_id, item_id, p FROM (SELECT user_id, item_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY t DESC, item_id) AS p FROM ev WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)) q WHERE p <= 10), es AS (SELECT e.user_id, e.item_id FROM e JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT item_id FROM s) si ON si.item_id = e.item_id), co AS (SELECT a.item_id AS i, b.item_id AS k, COUNT(*) AS c FROM es a JOIN es b ON b.user_id = a.user_id AND b.item_id <> a.item_id GROUP BY a.item_id, b.item_id), pr AS (SELECT x.user_id, y.p - x.p AS d, COALESCE(co.c / SQRT(n1.c * n2.c), 0) AS w FROM s x JOIN s y ON y.user_id = x.user_id AND y.p > x.p LEFT JOIN co ON co.i = x.item_id AND co.k = y.item_id LEFT JOIN n n1 ON n1.item_id = x.item_id LEFT JOIN n n2 ON n2.item_id = y.item_id) SELECT users.user_id, AVG(pr.w) AS f_x_c3_hist_cohesion, AVG(CASE WHEN pr.d = 1 THEN CASE WHEN pr.w > 0 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END END) AS f_x_c3_chain_support FROM users LEFT JOIN pr ON pr.user_id = users.user_id GROUP BY users.user_id;

rival.explanation: Cohesion falls mechanically with the popularity mix and the age of the user's items: popular and recent items have more co-users and therefore positive edges. The family may then only proxy ag_user_pop_pref and user activity.
rival.stratum: Mainstream heavy users: (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id) > 20

cards.name: neighbours_since_last_visit
cards.mechanism: A user-user neighbourhood anchored to the user's own clock. The neighbours of u are the top 30 users by cosine overlap with u's last 20 items in the last 90 steps. The value is the sim-weighted share of these neighbours who took j strictly after u's last interaction. A returning user tends to catch up on what their taste community adopted while they were away. A fixed 30-step window, as in ag_ucf30, mixes items that u has already passed over (adopted by neighbours while u was active and ignored) with items that are new to u. Cutting at u's last step separates the two.
cards.stratum: Lapsed users, active in the last 90 steps but not in the last 7: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id AND t >= {A} - 7) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id AND t >= {A} - 90)
cards.null_stratum: Users active in the last step, for whom nothing can happen after their last step and the value is 0: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id AND t >= {A} - 1)
cards.sql: WITH e AS (SELECT user_id, item_id, t FROM ev WHERE t >= {A} - 90), du AS (SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS c FROM e GROUP BY user_id), lt AS (SELECT user_id, MAX(t) AS tl FROM ev WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY user_id), s AS (SELECT user_id, item_id FROM (SELECT user_id, item_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY t DESC, item_id) AS p FROM e WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)) q WHERE p <= 20), ov AS (SELECT s.user_id AS u, e.user_id AS v, COUNT(*) AS c FROM s JOIN e ON e.item_id = s.item_id AND e.user_id <> s.user_id GROUP BY s.user_id, e.user_id), nb AS (SELECT ov.u, ov.v, ov.c / SQRT(a.c * b.c) AS w FROM ov JOIN du a ON a.user_id = ov.u JOIN du b ON b.user_id = ov.v QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ov.u ORDER BY ov.c / SQRT(a.c * b.c) DESC, ov.v) <= 30), tot AS (SELECT u, SUM(w) AS sw FROM nb GROUP BY u), ad AS (SELECT nb.u, e.item_id, SUM(nb.w) AS sw FROM nb JOIN lt ON lt.user_id = nb.u JOIN e ON e.user_id = nb.v AND e.t > lt.tl GROUP BY nb.u, e.item_id) SELECT cand.user_id, cand.item_id, COALESCE(ad.sw / tot.sw, 0) AS f_x_c3_nbr_since_share FROM cand LEFT JOIN tot ON tot.u = cand.user_id LEFT JOIN ad ON ad.u = cand.user_id AND ad.item_id = cand.item_id;

twin.sql: WITH e AS (SELECT user_id, item_id, t FROM ev WHERE t >= {A} - 90), du AS (SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS c FROM e GROUP BY user_id), ub AS (SELECT user_id, FLOOR(LOG2(c)) AS b, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY FLOOR(LOG2(c)) ORDER BY hash(user_id), user_id) AS r, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY FLOOR(LOG2(c))) AS m FROM du), um AS (SELECT x.user_id AS v, y.user_id AS v2 FROM ub x JOIN ub y ON y.b = x.b AND y.r = x.r % x.m + 1), lt AS (SELECT user_id, MAX(t) AS tl FROM ev WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY user_id), s AS (SELECT user_id, item_id FROM (SELECT user_id, item_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY t DESC, item_id) AS p FROM e WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)) q WHERE p <= 20), ov AS (SELECT s.user_id AS u, e.user_id AS v, COUNT(*) AS c FROM s JOIN e ON e.item_id = s.item_id AND e.user_id <> s.user_id GROUP BY s.user_id, e.user_id), nb AS (SELECT ov.u, ov.v, ov.c / SQRT(a.c * b.c) AS w FROM ov JOIN du a ON a.user_id = ov.u JOIN du b ON b.user_id = ov.v QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ov.u ORDER BY ov.c / SQRT(a.c * b.c) DESC, ov.v) <= 30), nb2 AS (SELECT nb.u, um.v2 AS v, nb.w FROM nb JOIN um ON um.v = nb.v), tot AS (SELECT u, SUM(w) AS sw FROM nb2 GROUP BY u), ad AS (SELECT nb2.u, e.item_id, SUM(nb2.w) AS sw FROM nb2 JOIN lt ON lt.user_id = nb2.u JOIN e ON e.user_id = nb2.v AND e.t > lt.tl GROUP BY nb2.u, e.item_id) SELECT cand.user_id, cand.item_id, COALESCE(ad.sw / tot.sw, 0) AS f_x_c3_nbr_since_share_tw FROM cand LEFT JOIN tot ON tot.u = cand.user_id LEFT JOIN ad ON ad.u = cand.user_id AND ad.item_id = cand.item_id;

rival.explanation: Any active users' adoptions after u's last step mostly reflect global popularity since that step. The gain may come from a 'popular since your last visit' window and not from the neighbourhood.
rival.stratum: Lapsed users with popular candidates: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id AND t >= {A} - 7) AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev WHERE ev.item_id = j.item_id AND t >= {A} - 30) >= 20

cards.name: item_successor_role
cards.mechanism: The position of an item in the transition graph. followup_share is the smoothed share of j's adoptions in the last 120 steps that came within 30 steps after the adopter's previous active step, so j has strong in-edges from other purchases. entry_share is the share of adoptions made in the adopter's very first step, an entry or source node. Every ranked user already has history, so the next item is by construction a transition from an earlier one. Items that are typically reached as follow-ups should rank higher than acquisition and entry items, which mostly attract new users and are counted by popularity anyway.
cards.stratum: Users in follow-up mode, active within the last 30 steps: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id AND t >= {A} - 30)
cards.null_stratum: Long-lapsed users who behave close to new entrants: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id AND t >= {A} - 90)

twin.sql: WITH E AS (SELECT user_id, item_id FROM ev WHERE t >= {A} - 180), L0 AS (SELECT user_id, item_id FROM (SELECT e.user_id, e.item_id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY e.user_id ORDER BY e.t DESC, e.item_id) AS rn FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)) x WHERE rn <= 10), n AS (SELECT item_id, count(*) AS c FROM E GROUP BY item_id), nb AS (SELECT item_id, floor(log2(c)) AS b, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY floor(log2(c)) ORDER BY item_id) AS r1, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY floor(log2(c)) ORDER BY hash(item_id), item_id) AS r2 FROM n), mp AS (SELECT x.item_id AS src, y.item_id AS dst FROM nb x JOIN nb y ON x.b = y.b AND x.r1 = y.r2), L AS (SELECT L0.user_id, mp.dst AS item_id FROM L0 JOIN mp ON mp.src = L0.item_id), co AS (SELECT a.item_id AS i, b.item_id AS j, count(*) AS c FROM E a JOIN E b ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND a.item_id <> b.item_id WHERE a.item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM L) AND b.item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM cand) GROUP BY a.item_id, b.item_id), s AS (SELECT L.user_id, co.j, sum(co.c) AS sc FROM L JOIN co ON co.i = L.item_id GROUP BY L.user_id, co.j) SELECT c.user_id, c.item_id, ln(1.0 + COALESCE(s.sc, 0)) AS f_x_c4_co_support_tw, COALESCE(s.sc, 0) / (COALESCE(n.c, 0) + 5.0) AS f_x_c4_co_share_j_tw FROM cand c LEFT JOIN s ON s.user_id = c.user_id AND s.j = c.item_id LEFT JOIN n ON n.item_id = c.item_id

rival.explanation: Raw support may only re-inject popularity times the user's history size: large-n items co-occur with everything. If so, the gain comes from popular candidates for heavy users, not from denoising cold items.
rival.stratum: users with n_items_all >= 30 and candidates with pop30_rank <= 20

cards.name: trendsetter_adopters
cards.mechanism: For cold items the audience is tiny, but who the adopters are carries information. Some users repeatedly take items within 14 steps of launch that later become popular; they act as scouts. Each user gets a score: the mean over their items launched before A-60 of ln(1 + users_all(i)) when taken early, and 0 otherwise. Items whose recent (last 60 steps) adopters are high-scoring scouts are about to spread and should be ranked up even when their own counts are small.
cards.stratum: young candidates with small audience: item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM ev GROUP BY item_id HAVING min(t) >= {A} - 60 AND count(*) <= 20)
cards.null_stratum: old saturated items: item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM ev GROUP BY item_id HAVING min(t) < {A} - 365 AND count(*) >= 500)
cards.sql: WITH f AS (SELECT item_id, min(t) AS ft, count(*) AS n FROM ev GROUP BY item_id), us AS (SELECT e.user_id, avg(CASE WHEN e.t - f.ft <= 14 THEN ln(1.0 + f.n) ELSE 0.0 END) AS sv FROM ev e JOIN f USING (item_id) WHERE f.ft < {A} - 60 GROUP BY e.user_id), ad AS (SELECT e.item_id, avg(COALESCE(us.sv, 0)) AS ms, sum(COALESCE(us.sv, 0)) AS ss FROM ev e LEFT JOIN us USING (user_id) WHERE e.t >= {A} - 60 GROUP BY e.item_id) SELECT item_id, ms AS f_x_c4_trendsetter_mean, ln(1.0 + ss) AS f_x_c4_trendsetter_sum FROM ad

twin.sql: WITH a AS (SELECT user_id, item_id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY hash(user_id, item_id), user_id, item_id) AS rk FROM ev), b AS (SELECT t, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY t, user_id, item_id) AS rk FROM ev), s AS (SELECT a.user_id, a.item_id, b.t FROM a JOIN b USING (rk)), f AS (SELECT item_id, min(t) AS ft, count(*) AS n FROM s GROUP BY item_id), us AS (SELECT s.user_id, avg(CASE WHEN s.t - f.ft <= 14 THEN ln(1.0 + f.n) ELSE 0.0 END) AS sv FROM s JOIN f USING (item_id) WHERE f.ft < {A} - 60 GROUP BY s.user_id), ad AS (SELECT e.item_id, avg(COALESCE(us.sv, 0)) AS ms, sum(COALESCE(us.sv, 0)) AS ss FROM ev e LEFT JOIN us USING (user_id) WHERE e.t >= {A} - 60 GROUP BY e.item_id) SELECT item_id, ms AS f_x_c4_trendsetter_mean_tw, ln(1.0 + ss) AS f_x_c4_trendsetter_sum_tw FROM ad

rival.explanation: Scout scores may mostly measure adopter activity (heavy users take many items early by chance), making the family a variant of adopter_depth that marks niche items.
rival.stratum: items with high ag_adopter_depth

cards.name: signup_cohort_affinity
cards.mechanism: Users acquired at the same time (same campaign, season or launch) share entry interests that history-based signals cannot see for a 1-3 item user. The cohort is the users whose first event lies within 3 steps of u's first event. The family gives the shrunk share of that cohort who took candidate j and its log lift over j's global penetration. This gives short-history users a personalised prior that does not depend on their few items having 180-step co-occurrence.
cards.stratum: recently acquired, short-history users: user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM ev GROUP BY user_id HAVING min(t) >= {A} - 60 AND count(*) <= 5)
cards.null_stratum: long-tenured heavy users, whose cohort is old and diluted: user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM ev GROUP BY user_id HAVING min(t) < {A} - 365 AND count(*) >= 30)
cards.sql: WITH uf AS (SELECT user_id, min(t) AS ft FROM ev GROUP BY user_id), fc AS (SELECT ft, count(*) AS n FROM uf GROUP BY ft), fi AS (SELECT uf.ft, e.item_id, count(*) AS c FROM ev e JOIN uf USING (user_id) WHERE e.item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM cand) GROUP BY uf.ft, e.item_id), cu AS (SELECT user_id, ft FROM uf WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), cn AS (SELECT cu.user_id, sum(fc.n) - 1 AS nn FROM cu JOIN fc ON fc.ft BETWEEN cu.ft - 3 AND cu.ft + 3 GROUP BY cu.user_id), ip AS (SELECT item_id, count(*) AS k FROM ev GROUP BY item_id), tot AS (SELECT count(*) AS m FROM uf), cc AS (SELECT c.user_id, c.item_id, sum(fi.c) AS kc FROM cand c JOIN cu ON cu.user_id = c.user_id JOIN fi ON fi.item_id = c.item_id AND fi.ft BETWEEN cu.ft - 3 AND cu.ft + 3 GROUP BY c.user_id, c.item_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.item_id, COALESCE(cc.kc, 0) / (cn.nn + 10.0) AS f_x_c4_cohort_share, ln((COALESCE(cc.kc, 0) + 1.0) / (cn.nn + 1.0)) - ln((ip.k + 1.0) / (tot.m + 1.0)) AS f_x_c4_cohort_lift FROM cand c JOIN cn ON cn.user_id = c.user_id JOIN ip ON ip.item_id = c.item_id CROSS JOIN tot LEFT JOIN cc ON cc.user_id = c.user_id AND cc.item_id = c.item_id

rival.explanation: For recent cohorts the share may simply equal recent popularity at sign-up time, a time-localised pop count. The gain would then mirror pop30 for new users rather than shared acquisition taste.
rival.stratum: users with user_age <= 30, where the cohort window overlaps [A-30, A)
